title: Destination City
spaceBreakdown:
- unordered_set<string> sources: up to n entries → O(n)
- recursion depth: none
- not counted: input paths, returned string
approach: The destination city is the one that appears as a destination (cityB) in some path but never as a source (cityA). Insert every cityA into a hash set, then scan the cityB values; the first one not in the set is the destination. This is correct because the graph is a line, so exactly one city has no outgoing edge.
hints: Each path is [source, destination]. What property does the final city have that no other city in the array has?
Use a hash set of all source cities (cityA). In Example 1, sources = {London, New York, Lima}; scanning destinations, "Sao Paulo" is not in the set, so it is the answer.

**Smallest input** - only one path exists.
`Input: [["A","Z"]]` → `Expected: "Z"`
⚠️ Bug: returning `paths.back()[1]` works here but is fragile; a correct set-based check still returns "Z".

**Shuffled order** - paths are not given in trip order.
`Input: [["C","D"],["A","B"],["B","C"]]` → `Expected: "D"`
⚠️ Bug: returning `paths.back()[1]` → returns "C" instead of "D".

**City names with spaces** - names contain the space character.
`Input: [["New York","Sao Paulo"]]` → `Expected: "Sao Paulo"`
⚠️ Bug: splitting names on spaces or trimming them → returns "Sao" or "Paulo".

**Count-based check** - a city appearing once is not necessarily the destination.
`Input: [["London","New York"],["New York","Lima"],["Lima","Sao Paulo"]]` → `Expected: "Sao Paulo"`
⚠️ Bug: returning the city that appears exactly once overall → returns "London" instead of "Sao Paulo".

followUps.q: If the graph were a general DAG with possibly multiple sinks, how would you return all destination cities?
followUps.a: Build the same source set, then collect every cityB not in it. Time stays O(n); the output list can hold up to O(n) cities.

followUps.q: If paths arrive as an unbounded stream and you cannot store all of them, how would you find the destination?
followUps.a: Keep two hash sets: candidates (cities seen only as destinations so far) and sources. On each new [a,b], remove b from candidates if a was already a source-side city, add a to sources, and add b to candidates if it is not in sources. At end of stream, candidates holds the destination. Space is O(number of distinct cities seen).

followUps.q: If city names could be up to 10^6 characters each, how does the complexity change?
followUps.a: Hashing and comparing a string of length L costs O(L), so total time becomes O(total characters) and the set still uses O(n) entries but each entry stores a long string (or a hash digest to save space).
